passages.t: Sin engraved on the heart, and a tree by the water
passages.happening:
‘The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, engraved with a diamond point on the tablets of their hearts and on the horns of their altars’ (verse 1). Even their children remember the altars and the Asherah poles by the green trees (verse 2). Their wealth will be plunder, and they will lose the land God gave them (verses 3 and 4).

‘Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind, who makes the flesh his strength and turns his heart from the LORD’ (verse 5). He is like a shrub in the desert, in a salt land where no one lives (verse 6). But the one who trusts in the LORD, whose confidence is in him (verse 7), ‘is like a tree planted by the waters that sends out its roots toward the stream’ (verse 8). It does not fear the heat, and in a year of drought it keeps bearing fruit.

‘The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Who can understand it?’ (verse 9). ‘I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind to reward a man according to his way’ (verse 10). The one who grows rich unjustly is like a partridge sitting on eggs it did not lay; his riches will leave him (verse 11). The LORD is the hope of Israel, ‘the fountain of living water’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
An iron stylus with a diamond point was a tool for cutting inscriptions into stone or metal, writing meant to last. The horns of the altar were the projections at its four corners, where the priest smeared blood for cleansing. Judah's sin is cut into the very places that were meant to take sin away.

The Asherah poles were wooden objects linked with the goddess Asherah. Josiah had tried to clear them away in the 620s BC, but the local shrines had come back.

The two plants of verses 5 to 8 would be familiar to anyone who knew the land: the scrubby bush of the salt desert near the Dead Sea, and the tree on a riverbank whose roots reach water even in drought. The contrast is the same as Psalm 1.

The partridge in verse 11 was believed in popular lore to hatch eggs that were not its own, only for the chicks to leave it. So ill-gotten wealth does not stay.
passages.later: The first psalm uses the same picture: ‘He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season’ (Psalm 1:3). Another psalm prays, ‘Search me, O God, and know my heart’ (Psalm 139:23).
passages.asks: The heart is deceitful, and only God searches it. Ask what in your own heart you may be fooling yourself about. And ask where your roots go when the heat comes: toward the stream, or toward your own strength.

passages.t: A prayer for healing and refuge
passages.happening:
Jeremiah prays. ‘Heal me, O LORD, and I will be healed; save me, and I will be saved, for You are my praise’ (verse 14). People keep mocking him, asking where the word of the LORD is and telling it to come now (verse 15).

He has not run from being God's shepherd, and he has not wished for the day of disaster; God knows what he has said (verse 16). ‘Do not become a terror to me; You are my refuge in the day of disaster’ (verse 17). He asks that his persecutors be put to shame and terrified, and that he not be (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This is the third of Jeremiah's confessions, short and sharp. His enemies mocked him because the disaster he announced had not yet come. Their taunt, Where is the word of the LORD?, meant that his warnings were empty.

Jeremiah protests that he never wanted the day of disaster. He announced it because he had to, not because he enjoyed it. A prophet who longs for judgment on his own people is no prophet of God.

His prayer for his persecutors' shame is honest and harsh. He does not take revenge into his own hands. He brings it to God.
passages.later: A psalm prays the same: ‘Heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony’ (Psalm 6:2). Peter warns of mockers who will ask, “Where is the promise of His coming?” (2 Peter 3:4).
passages.asks: Jeremiah asked God to heal and save him, sure that only God could. Ask what healing you need that only God can give. And ask whether you have ever wanted the downfall of someone you were warning.

passages.t: Keep the Sabbath at the gates
passages.happening:
God tells Jeremiah to stand at the gate of the people, where the kings of Judah go in and out, and at all the gates of Jerusalem (verse 19). ‘Do not carry a load or bring it through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day’ (verse 21). They must keep the Sabbath holy, as God commanded their fathers, who would not listen (verses 22 and 23).

If they listen and keep the Sabbath, kings on David's throne will ride through these gates, and the city will be inhabited forever (verses 24 and 25). People will come from all Judah and Benjamin bringing offerings and thanksgiving to the house of the LORD (verse 26). But if they do not listen, God will kindle a fire in the gates that will consume Jerusalem's fortresses and not be put out (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The gate of the people is not known today. The concern is plain: trade carried on through the city gates on the day of rest. The Sabbath protected servants, workers and animals from endless labor, and it was a sign of the covenant.

Keeping it meant stopping, trusting God for what a day's trade would have brought. Breaking it showed a people who would not stop for God or anyone.

Nehemiah faced the same problem after the return, with goods carried into Jerusalem on the Sabbath, and shut the gates to stop it.
passages.later: Nehemiah saw goods being ‘brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day’ (Nehemiah 13:15) and shut the gates. Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter make the whole city's fate depend on a rule about carrying loads, and how should Christians apply it?

Verses 24 to 27 can sound as though Jerusalem's survival hangs on one regulation. But in Jeremiah the Sabbath works as a test of the whole covenant: whether the people would stop, listen and trust God rather than their own work and trade. The prophets never treat Sabbath-keeping as a substitute for justice. They treat its neglect as a symptom of a heart that has stopped listening.

How Christians apply the command is a second-order question on which faithful traditions differ. Some hold that the Sabbath principle carries over to the Lord's Day, Sunday, as a day of worship and rest. Others keep the seventh day itself. Others read the New Testament (Colossians 2:16-17; Hebrews 4) as saying the Sabbath is fulfilled in the rest Christ gives, leaving the keeping of days to conscience (Romans 14:5-6).
passages.asks: The Sabbath asked the people to stop trading and trust God. Ask whether you ever stop, and what you fear losing if you do. And ask who works without rest so that your life can go on, and whether they rest too.
